passages.t: ‘Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?’ The right to be supported
passages.happening:
Paul has just said he would give up meat for a brother's sake (8:13). Now he shows that he lives this way already. He opens with four questions. “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord?” (verse 1). The church in Corinth is itself the proof of his work: “you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord” (verse 2).

Then he gives his defence. He and Barnabas have the same rights as the other apostles: food and drink, and the right “to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas” (verse 5). “Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?” (verse 6).

He argues from ordinary life. A soldier is paid, a man who plants a vineyard eats its grapes, and a shepherd drinks the milk of his flock (verse 7). Then from the Law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (verse 9). The one who sows should share in the harvest. “If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?” (verse 11).

Then the turn. “But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
An apostle is ‘one who is sent’, a messenger with authority from the one who sent him. Some in Corinth seem to have doubted that Paul was a real apostle. One reason, it appears, was money. In 2 Corinthians the complaint is out in the open: “Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” (2 Corinthians 11:7).

In the Greek and Roman world a travelling teacher could live in several ways. He could charge fees. He could join the household of a rich patron, a wealthy man who gave support and expected loyalty in return. He could beg. Or he could work at a trade. Paul chose the last. Acts says that in Corinth he worked with Aquila and Priscilla, “because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was” (Acts 18:3). Believers from Macedonia also sent him help (2 Corinthians 11:9). People of rank looked down on hand work, so his choice cost him standing in the eyes of some.

Verse 5 gives a small glimpse of the first church leaders. Cephas is Peter's Aramaic name, and the Gospels mention his mother-in-law (Mark 1:30), so he was married. Here we learn that his wife travelled with him. ‘The Lord's brothers’ are the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospels, among them James, who later led the church in Jerusalem. Barnabas had been Paul's partner on his first long mission (Acts 13 and 14), and it seems he too worked for his keep.

The word ‘right’ in this chapter is exousia, authority or right. It comes six times. It is the same word the strong in Corinth used for their freedom to eat in 8:9. Paul has a right as real as theirs. He is about to show what he does with it.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes the Law: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4). An ox walked round and round over the cut grain, or pulled a sledge over it, to break the heads loose. A muzzle would stop it eating as it worked. The Law said let it eat.

Paul asks, “Is it about oxen that God is concerned?” (verse 9). He is not saying God does not care for animals. The Old Testament says he does. He is reasoning from the smaller to the greater: if God provides for an ox that works, how much more for people who work. It is worth noticing that the verse sits among laws about people. Just before it is a law that limits how many lashes a guilty man may receive, “lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight” (Deuteronomy 25:3). The ox law is part of a picture of fairness and dignity.

The same verse is quoted again in 1 Timothy, beside a saying of Jesus: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages” (1 Timothy 5:18). Jesus said those words when he sent out his followers (Luke 10:7).
passages.hard:
What does this passage teach about paying pastors?

Paul says plainly that those who preach have a right to be supported by those they serve, and that this right rests on common sense, on the Law and on a command of Jesus (verse 14). Most churches pay their pastors and other ministers for that reason. Nothing here counts that as wrong or second best.

Paul also shows that a minister may choose not to use the right, as he did in Corinth, for the sake of the gospel. Many ministers today work another job as well, some by need and some by choice, and Paul's example honours them too.

The passage does not set a rule for how much a minister should be paid, or how a church should arrange it. Churches do it in many ways. And nothing here gives anyone a licence to demand money for the gospel or to grow rich from it. Paul's whole point runs the other way: he would rather go without than let money get in the way of the message. Peter warned the elders to shepherd the flock “not out of greed, but out of eagerness” (1 Peter 5:2).
passages.asks: Paul had a real right and set it aside so that nothing would get in the way of the gospel. Ask what rights you hold on to most tightly. And if you belong to a church, ask whether those who serve you are cared for as Paul says they should be.

passages.t: ‘I would rather die’: the gospel free of charge
passages.happening:
Paul gives two more reasons for the right. Those who serve in the temple eat from its food, and those who serve at the altar share in its offerings (verse 13). “In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (verse 14).

“But I have not used any of these rights” (verse 15). He is not writing to ask for money now. He would rather die than lose his boast.

Yet preaching itself is nothing to boast about. “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (verse 16). He was not given a choice. If he preached of his own will, he would have a reward. But it is a task he has been trusted with (verse 17).

“What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Everyone in Corinth knew that those who served at a temple ate from its sacrifices. That was true of the temples of the gods in their own city, and true of the temple in Jerusalem. Paul could point to both.

‘The Lord has prescribed’ points to a teaching of Jesus. When Jesus sent out his followers to preach, he told them to eat what they were given, “For the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). Matthew records the same saying with ‘provisions’ (Matthew 10:10). Paul knew the words of Jesus and treated them as a command with authority.

So Paul's choice was not a refusal of what Jesus taught. It was a choice not to use a right Jesus gave. Why would he make it? He says why: so the gospel would come ‘free of charge’. In a city where teachers were paid by fees or by patrons, Paul did not want anyone to think he was selling a product. And he did not want to be bound to any rich member of the church as that man's client.

Verse 17 uses the language of a household. ‘Entrusted with a responsibility’ translates a word for being given the management of a household, the oikonomia, the work a trusted slave or steward did for his master. A steward did not choose his task, and he was not paid extra for doing it. Paul says that is what preaching is for him. His only ‘reward’ is to give it away.
passages.ot:
The priests and Levites of Israel lived from the offerings. One law says the whole tribe of Levi “shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They are to eat the offerings made by fire to the LORD; that is their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18:1). Another says of the Levites' share, “it is the compensation for your work at the Tent of Meeting” (Numbers 18:31).

Paul's ‘Woe to me if I do not preach’ sounds like the prophets, who spoke because they could not keep quiet. Jeremiah tried to stop, and God's word became “a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9). Amos put it as a question. The Lord GOD has spoken, he says, and then: “who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8). Paul stands in that line. The call was not his idea.
passages.asks: Paul found his reward in giving the gospel away. Ask what you expect to get back for the good you do, even if it is only thanks or notice. And ask whether there is anything in how you speak of Christ that might make it look like something sold rather than a gift.

passages.happening:
“Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible” (verse 19).

“To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews” (verse 20). To those under the law he lived like one under the law, though he himself is not under the law. To those without the law he lived like one without the law, “though I am not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ” (verse 21).

“To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (verse 22). “I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
‘Win’ is kerdainō, a word from trade for making a profit. Paul uses it five times in four verses. He had turned down money. The gain he wants is people.

To make yourself a slave was shocking to free people in Corinth. Slaves had no rights of their own. Paul, a free man and a Roman citizen, says he has chosen to put himself at everyone's service.

What did this look like? With Jews, Paul kept Jewish customs, such as the food laws and the feasts. Acts tells that he had Timothy circumcised “on account of the Jews in that area” (Acts 16:3), and that in Jerusalem he joined four men who had taken a vow and went with them into the temple (Acts 21:26). With Gentiles he ate their food and did not ask them to become Jews. With ‘the weak’, the believers of chapter 8 with a tender conscience, he gave up what he was free to do.

But he puts limits on it, and he states them in the same breath. He is never ‘outside the law of God’. He is ‘under the law of Christ’, the way of life Jesus taught and lived. Elsewhere Paul says, “Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The message never changes. The messenger bends.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knows of a servant who gives himself for many. Isaiah speaks of the LORD's servant who suffers for others: “He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). Jesus took that path: “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Paul says the same of Christ, who “emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). Paul's ‘slave to everyone’ copies his Lord.

‘Under the law’ means the Law of Moses as the rule a Jew lived by. Paul honours that Law and quotes it often, as in this chapter (Deuteronomy 25:4). But he says believers in Christ, Jew or Gentile, are not under it as the covenant that rules them. They belong to Christ.
passages.hard:
Isn't ‘all things to all people’ just a way of telling people what they want to hear?

Paul's critics may have thought so. But look at what he changes and what he does not. He changes customs the gospel leaves free: what he eats, which days he keeps, whether he takes pay, how he lives among different peoples. He does not change the message of Christ crucified (2:2). He will not join in worship of idols (10:14-22). And when bending to one group would have harmed the gospel for another, he refused to bend. He opposed Peter to his face over that very thing: “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?” (Galatians 2:14).

So the verse is not a licence to blend in with anything, or to hide the hard parts of the faith to be liked. Paul also wrote, “If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). The point is the reverse of pleasing people. It is giving up your own comfort and preferences so that others can hear.

Christians have always had to judge where meeting people where they are serves the gospel and where it empties it. Missionaries learning a language and eating local food stand on one side of that line. A message changed to suit the hearers stands on the other. Paul's example is both a permission and a limit.
passages.asks: Paul gave up his own preferences so that others could hear. Ask who in your life is far from you in culture, age or habits. What would it mean to become ‘like’ them, without leaving Christ behind? And ask the harder question: have you ever changed the message itself to be liked?

passages.happening:
“Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize” (verse 24).

“Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable” (verse 25).

“Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air” (verse 26). “No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, one of the great festivals of the Greek world, held every two years. Paul's hearers did not need athletics explained. They knew the runners, the boxers and the months of hard training.

The winner's prize was a crown, a wreath of leaves. At the Isthmian Games it was made of celery or of pine, at different times in its history. Within days it would wither. Paul's word for crown here is stephanos, the victor's wreath, not a king's crown. ‘Imperishable’ means it will never wither or decay.

‘I do not fight like I am beating the air’ is a picture from boxing: a fighter swinging at nothing, or shadow-boxing. ‘Discipline my body’ uses a strong word, hypōpiazō, for landing a blow, as a boxer does. Paul means hard training, not harming the body. He has just spent a chapter giving up food, pay and comfort. That is his training.

‘Disqualified’ is adokimos, failing the test, the word for a coin found to be false or a competitor ruled out. Paul uses the same word in his next letter to the Corinthians: “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves” (2 Corinthians 13:5).

This race is not one where only one runner wins and the rest lose. Paul's point in verse 24 is the effort, not the competition. Run like someone who means to win.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament uses running for the life of faith. “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). The psalmist says, “I run in the path of Your commandments” (Psalm 119:32).

Paul's other letters take up the same picture. “I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14). And near the end of his life: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).
passages.hard:
‘I myself will not be disqualified’ (verse 27). Could Paul, the apostle, have been lost? Christians who read the Bible faithfully answer in different ways.

Much of the Reformed and Baptist world holds that those truly saved are kept by God and cannot finally be lost (John 10:28). Some of them read ‘disqualified’ as losing a reward or being set aside from service, not losing salvation. Others say the warning is real and is one of the very means God uses to keep his people running.

Much of the Wesleyan, Arminian and Catholic world holds that a believer can turn away and be lost. They read Paul as taking that danger seriously even for himself, and they point to the warnings that follow in chapter 10 and to Hebrews 6:4-6.

These notes do not choose. Both readings agree that Paul did not treat his calling as a guarantee that let him stop running. Both, rightly held, lead to the same place: a humble clinging to Christ, not careless presumption and not gnawing fear. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’, sets out both.

If you are afraid you have already been disqualified, notice that Paul writes this to keep people running, not to make them give up. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust.
passages.asks: Athletes give up a great deal for a crown that withers. Ask what you are training for, and what your days show about it. Then ask what one habit, given up or taken up, would help you run this week with purpose and not just beat the air.
